what_it_does: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) are a cryptographic technique that lets one party convince another that a statement is true without revealing any secret information — think proving you know a password without ever saying the password. Running ZKP protocols requires several different kinds of heavy math, including a transform called Number Theoretic Transform (a way of doing fast arithmetic over large numbers), hash functions, and general polynomial (algebraic) calculations. Existing custom chips built to speed up ZKPs were each designed for a single older style of ZKP math and cannot efficiently handle the newer hash-based protocols, leaving large portions of the chip idle. UniZK redesigns the underlying hardware as a flexible, reconfigurable grid of small multiplier units — similar to how a spreadsheet of cells can each pass results to neighbors — and adds extra local connections plus a new mode that lets the same grid act as different specialized processors for each type of math. New strategies then intelligently route each computation across that shared grid so resources stay busy regardless of which ZKP operation is running.
